title: Why compound interest wins
blurb: Interest lands on top of interest, so money grows faster the longer it sits. You'll see what $1,000 does at 8% a year, and the one-line trick for knowing when it doubles.
takeaway: You learned why time matters more than amount.

cards.body: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Like a snowball rolling downhill, the money grows faster the longer it goes.
Put $1,000 in an account paying 8% a year. Twelve months later it has grown by $80. Nothing clever yet. That is just the rate doing its job.
Year 2 you earn $86, not $80. The $80 from last year is sitting in the account now, so it earns interest too. That extra $6 is the whole trick.
Leave it alone. Year 10 it’s $2,159. Year 20, $4,661. Year 30, over $10,000. All from $1,000 you never touched.
A flat $80 a year would give you $3,400 after 30 years. Interest on interest gives you $10,063. That gap is compounding.
Divide 72 by the rate to see how long doubling takes. At 8%, that’s 9 years: $1,000, $2,000, $4,000, $8,000.
Two people both put away $200 a month, every month, into the same kind of account. One starts at 18. The other waits and starts at 28.
By 60, the one who started at 18 has about $824,000. The one who started at 28 has about $355,000.
The early saver only put in $24,000 more. Time did the rest. The extra ten years let the interest pile up on itself.
Starting at 18 instead of 28 can roughly double what you end up with. Time matters more than amount.
It works against you too. Credit card debt compounds the same way, often at 25%. A small balance rolls into a big one.

cards.question: Why does year 2 earn more than year 1?
choices: You added more money to the account during the year.
The interest from year 1 is now earning interest too.
The bank raises the rate a little each year you stay.
cards.why: Interest is added to your balance, so year 2 is worked out on $1,080 instead of $1,000. Nothing else changed.

title: Your first budget in 4 lines
blurb: A budget is a plan you make before you spend, not a punishment you write after. Four lines is enough to start, and one of them does most of the work.
takeaway: You learned that the savings line should move on its own.

cards.body: A budget is just a plan for money before you spend it. Four lines is enough to start.
Half goes to needs. Rent, food, the bus. That's the 50.
Thirty percent is wants. Not a moral failing, just a planned amount.
The last fifth is savings. That's the line that actually changes anything.
Track one month before you set the numbers. Most people are shocked by one category, and that category is your lever.
Automate the savings line. If it moves on payday, you never have to be disciplined.

cards.question: Why automate savings instead of saving what's left over?
choices: Banks pay more on automatic transfers
Nothing is left over at the end of the month
cards.why: Money you can see is money you spend. Moving it first makes the plan happen without willpower.

title: What an emergency fund is for
blurb: The point of an emergency fund is not the interest. It's that a flat tyre stops being a crisis and starts being an errand.
takeaway: You learned what cash is for when something breaks.

cards.body: An emergency fund is cash you keep boring on purpose. Not invested, not locked up. Just there.
A $400 repair with the cash there is an errand. You pay it and forget it.
The same $400 on a card at 24% is a crisis that follows you into June.
Start with $500. That covers most of what actually goes wrong: a phone, a tyre, a co-pay.
An emergency fund buys you the right to say no to bad borrowing.

cards.question: Why keep an emergency fund in plain cash instead of investing it?
choices: You need it on the day you need it
Investing it is against the rules
cards.why: Investments can be down exactly when your car breaks. The job of this money is to be available, not to grow.

title: Credit scores, plainly
blurb: A credit score is a guess about whether you pay people back. Two of the five inputs do most of the work, and both are in your control.
takeaway: You learned that paying on time beats paying it all.

cards.body: A credit score is one number that guesses how likely you are to pay back what you borrow.
It runs from about 300 to 850. Most people sit somewhere in the middle.
Paying on time is the heaviest input by a distance. One late mark costs you for years.
Second is how much of your limit you use. Under 30% is the usual advice; under 10% is better.
Paying on time is worth more than paying it all off. One late payment costs more than a big balance.

cards.question: You can only do one this month. Which helps your score more?
choices: Pay the full balance a week late
cards.why: Payment history is the heaviest single input. A late mark sits on your report for years; a carried balance does not.

title: Good debt, bad debt
blurb: Debt isn't good or bad by nature. It's a price you pay for time, and the question is only ever whether you're buying something worth more than the price.
takeaway: You learned to ask what the debt buys before you take it.

cards.body: All debt is renting money. The interest rate is the rent.
A rate is just a price. 24% a year means if you owe $1,000 for a year, $240 of that is the fee for owing it. Nothing you bought got better. That's rent.
Rent is worth paying when the thing you bought is worth more later. A degree. A business.
Careful with that one though. A degree is worth it if you finish it and it leads somewhere. Debt for a course you drop out of is the same debt with none of the payoff.
It almost never is when the thing shrinks: a night out, a phone, a weekend.
Here's what that looks like. Put $1,000 on a card at 24% and pay the $25 minimum. It takes almost seven years. You pay back $2,032 in total. Half of that is rent on a night you already forgot.

If you owe on more than one thing, write them all down with their rates. Pay the minimum on every one. Then throw every spare dollar at the highest rate. That order saves you the most money, every time.

Watch out for the deal that isn't one. Zero percent for twelve months is still debt with a deadline. Some of those charge you all the skipped interest at once if you're late or still owe anything at the end.
Ask one question: will this still be worth something when I finish paying for it?

cards.question: A credit card charges 24% a year. A savings account pays 4%. What should a spare $100 do first?
cards.why: Paying off 24% debt is a guaranteed 24% return. No savings account can beat that.

title: Why index funds beat picking
blurb: Most professional stock pickers lose to a fund that buys everything and thinks about nothing. Here's why that keeps happening.
takeaway: You learned why the boring fund keeps winning.

cards.body: An index fund buys a slice of every company on a list, then does nothing else.

First, what a fund is. It's a big bucket lots of people put money into. The bucket buys things. You own a slice of the bucket. An index fund's rule is the simplest one there is: buy everything on the list, then leave it alone.
Picking one company means being right about that one, twice, for twenty years.

Twice, because you have to buy at the right time and sell at the right time. Getting one of those right is luck. Getting both right, over and over, is what full-time professionals are paid to do. Most of them fail at it.
Over twenty years most professional pickers land behind the boring fund. Fees eat the difference.

Fees sound tiny and aren't. Put $10,000 in for twenty years at 7% and you end up with about $38,700. Charge 1% a year in fees and it's about $32,100. That 1% quietly took $6,600, which is 17% of everything you made.
So when you look at a fund, find the number called the expense ratio. That's the yearly fee. Broad index funds are often under 0.1%. Anything over 1% needs to explain itself.
The other mistake is checking it. The fund will drop, sometimes a lot. Selling then is how you lock the loss in. The boring plan only works if you're boring about it.
The boring fund wins because it costs almost nothing and never panics.

cards.question: Why do fees matter so much over 20 years?
choices: Fees come out of the money that would have compounded
cards.why: Every dollar in fees is a dollar that stops earning. Over decades a 1% fee quietly takes a large slice of the total.

title: Stoicism: control what you can
blurb: The Stoics split the world in two and told you to spend your energy on one half. It's two thousand years old and it maps almost exactly onto a bad exam week.
takeaway: You learned to spend your energy on the half you control.

cards.body: Stoics split the world in two: things you control, and things you don't.
Your effort and your reaction are the first group. Those are always yours.
A posted grade, a curve, what somebody else scored. All second group. Epictetus said suffering comes from trying to control those.
A grade is already up. Refreshing the page is the second group. Emailing to ask what you missed is the first.
Before you stress, ask: is this in my control? If no, let it go. If yes, act on it today.

cards.question: Which of these is in the first group, the part you control?
cards.why: Your effort is yours. The curve and other people's scores are outcomes you can influence at best, never control.

title: The Socratic method
blurb: Socrates never told anyone the answer. He asked until they noticed they didn't have one. It turns out that is the fastest way to find out what you actually know.
takeaway: You learned that asking why beats reading again.

cards.body: Socrates taught by asking questions, not giving answers. Start with something you believe.
Socrates was a teacher in Athens about 2,400 years ago. He wrote nothing down. His method was to keep asking people to explain what they'd just said. Either it held up, or it didn't.
Ask why once and you get a reason. That part is usually easy.

Try it on something small. 'I should use flashcards.' Why? 'Because they help me remember.' Why do they? 'Because I test myself.' Why does testing work? Three questions in, you either know or you've found the hole.
Ask why twice and most beliefs run out of floor. That is not a failure. That's the method working.
It feels bad, and it's supposed to. Finding out you can't explain something you were sure about is uncomfortable. That discomfort is the only reliable sign you've found something worth studying.
Use it on your own notes. Cover the page and ask why the answer is the answer. If you can only say what the answer is, you've memorised a shape and not an idea.
One warning. This is a tool for checking your own thinking, not for winning arguments. Asking someone why five times in a row doesn't make you Socrates. It makes you annoying.
Asking why this is the answer beats rereading the answer.

cards.question: Why does asking 'why' beat rereading your notes?
choices: It forces you to produce the reason instead of recognise it
cards.why: Recognising something feels like knowing it. Producing the reason from memory is the thing a test actually asks for.

title: Occam's razor
blurb: The oldest debugging tool there is: when two explanations both fit, start with the one that assumes less. It isn't a law of nature, and that matters too.
takeaway: You learned which explanation to test first.

cards.body: Occam's razor: when two explanations fit the same facts, start with the one that assumes less.
It's named after William of Ockham. He was a monk who argued you shouldn't invent extra things to explain something if you don't need them. A razor because it shaves off what you don't need.
Your code broke after you changed one line. That line is one assumption.
Count the assumptions and the choice makes itself. 'I typed it wrong' assumes one thing. 'The compiler has a bug nobody else has hit' assumes four. Both could be true. One is far cheaper to check.
A compiler bug is four. It might still be right. It is just more expensive to check.
So the razor is an order, not an answer. Check the cheap one first. If it holds, you're done in a minute. If it doesn't, you've lost a minute and you now know something.

The common misuse is treating simplest as truest. Sometimes the weird explanation is the real one. The razor doesn't say it's wrong. It says check the boring one before you spend a day on the interesting one.
Try it the next time something breaks. Write the two explanations down. Count what each one needs to be true. Test the smaller number first, every time.
The simplest explanation isn't the truest. It's the one worth checking first.

cards.question: What does the razor actually tell you to do?
cards.why: It ranks what to check, not what is true. A complicated explanation can still win once the simple one fails.

title: The veil of ignorance
blurb: John Rawls' test for whether a rule is fair: design it before you know who you'll be under it.
takeaway: You learned a test for whether a rule is actually fair.

cards.body: John Rawls asked: what rules would you write if you didn't know who you'd be under them?
You keep everything you know about how the world works. You lose only who you are in it.
Then you get handed a life at random and have to live under the rule you just wrote.
Would you set the late-work policy the same way if you didn't know whether you'd be the student with a job after school?
A fair rule is one you'd still write if you didn't know which side of it you'd land on.

cards.question: What is the veil hiding from you?
choices: Which position in society you'll occupy
cards.why: You keep full knowledge of how the world works. You lose only the knowledge of who you'll be in it.

title: The map is not the territory
blurb: Every model leaves things out on purpose. Trouble starts when you forget which things.
takeaway: You learned to ask what a model left out.

cards.body: A map is useful because it leaves things out. A map with everything on it would be the size of the world.
Every model does this: a formula, a stereotype, a study guide. Something got cut to make it usable.
The skill is knowing what was cut, and whether you needed it.
A practice test predicts your real score well. It still can't tell you that you always slow down on the last section.
Ask what a model left out before you trust what it says.

cards.question: What makes a map useful?
choices: It leaves the right things out
cards.why: Detail is what makes a map unusable. The skill is knowing which detail was dropped and whether you needed it.

title: Spaced practice beats cramming
blurb: Same total hours, very different results. Splitting study across days works because forgetting a little is part of how remembering gets strong.
takeaway: You learned that the gap between sessions does the work.

cards.body: The night before a test, one long cram. Three hours, one desk, one energy drink. It all goes in fast, and it feels like it is working.
And it leaks just as fast. By the next morning some of it is already gone. A week later, most of what you crammed has gone with it.
Spacing means splitting the time you were going to spend anyway. Not more hours. The same hour, cut into pieces, with days between them.
Split the same hour over six days. Each ten-minute session catches the memory just before it slips, and lifts it a little higher than last time.
Your brain strengthens a memory each time it nearly forgets it, then pulls it back. A memory you never have to reach for stays weak.
Cramming feels better and works worse. When it's all fresh, recalling is easy, so you feel like you know it. The ease is the problem.
Put the sessions in your calendar the day you get the material. Ten minutes each, a day apart. If it is not on the calendar, it will not happen.
This lesson can't save you tonight. If the test is tomorrow, cram, then get some sleep. Space the next one and feel the difference.
Anything you have to remember: vocab, formulas, dates, names. It also works for skills like problem sets, as long as you spread the practice out.
The gap between sessions is doing the work, not the sessions.

cards.question: Why does leaving a gap between study sessions help?
choices: You come back rested, so you can focus for longer.
Partly forgetting makes each recall count for more.
Shorter sessions are easier to fit into a busy week.
cards.why: Rest and fit are nice, but they are not the mechanism. Each time you nearly forget and pull it back, the memory gets stronger.

title: How to study for a science quiz
blurb: Science quizzes ask you to explain a mechanism, not to recognise a term. Three passes over two evenings does more than one long night with a highlighter.
takeaway: You learned to draw the mechanism instead of highlighting it.

cards.body: A science quiz almost never asks you to recognise a word. Highlighting the definition feels like work and isn't.
Draw the mechanism instead: two sides, which one is saltier, and which way the water goes.
If you can draw it from memory, you can answer any wording of the question.
Don't memorise 'osmosis: movement of water'. Draw the two sides, mark which is saltier, then draw the arrow.
If you can draw the mechanism from memory, you're ready. Highlighting is not studying.

cards.question: You have two evenings before the quiz. What's the better use of night one?
choices: Write what you remember, then check
cards.why: Writing it first shows you the gaps. Rereading shows you familiar pages and hides what you don't know.

title: Active recall in ten minutes
blurb: The single highest-value ten minutes in studying, and it needs no app, no cards, and no colour coding.
takeaway: You learned to start with a blank page, every time.

cards.body: Active recall means pulling something out of your head, not putting it back in.
There's a difference between knowing something and recognising it. You recognise a face you can't name. Rereading notes trains recognising. Exams ask you to name.
The whole method: close everything, write what you remember, then check what you missed.
Ten minutes, for real. Two minutes shutting the laptop and the notes. Five minutes writing everything you can remember on a blank page. Three minutes opening the notes and marking what wasn't there.
The part you missed is your entire study list. Everything else is already learned.
This is why rereading fools people. It feels smooth and quick, and that smoothness gets mistaken for knowing. A blank page feels awful because it's actually measuring you.
You don't need materials for it. Walking to class, try to list the four things from the last lecture. Whatever you can't get is what you open the notes to later.
The mistake is checking too early. If you peek the second it gets hard, you've turned it back into reading. Sit in the blank for a bit. That struggle is the part that works.
Blank page first, notes second. Always in that order.

cards.question: Rereading your notes feels much easier than a blank page. Why is that a warning sign?
choices: Easy means you already know it
Recognising is easier than remembering, and only one is tested
Notes are shorter than the textbook
cards.why: Familiarity feels like knowledge. A blank page is uncomfortable precisely because it measures the thing a test measures.

title: Mix the problems up
blurb: Doing twenty of the same problem type teaches you to run one method. Mixing them teaches you to pick one, which is the harder half.
takeaway: You learned to practise choosing the method, not just running it.

cards.body: Most problem sets are blocked: four of type A, then four of type B.
That trains running a method. Mixing them up trains choosing one, which is the harder half.
On the test nothing is labelled. Practise the part that isn't labelled.
Do 5 of A, 5 of B, then shuffle 10 together. The shuffled ten are where the test actually lives.
On the test nothing is labelled. Practise the part that isn't labelled.

cards.question: Why does mixed practice feel worse than blocked practice?
choices: You make more mistakes while you're learning to choose
cards.why: Struggling to pick the right method is the skill being built. The mistakes are the training, not a sign it isn't working.

title: How to read a chapter once
blurb: Reading a chapter twice is usually reading it badly once, twice. Three moves make one pass enough.
takeaway: You learned to read once, with a question in hand.

cards.body: Before reading, turn every heading into a question. 'Cell division' becomes 'how does a cell divide?'
The reason is simple. Reading with no question is just moving your eyes over a page and hoping. A question gives your brain something to look for, so it notices when the answer shows up.
Now you're searching for an answer instead of scanning a page, and you notice it when it arrives.
Do it out loud with the contents page first. Six headings become six questions. That takes about two minutes and it's the whole setup.
At the end, write four sentences with the book shut. That's your whole set of notes.
Shut is the important word. If the book is open you'll copy, and copying feels like working while teaching you nothing. Four sentences from memory beats two pages of transcription.
If a section has no headings, use the first line of each paragraph instead. Same trick. You're just looking for what this bit is trying to tell me.

The mistake is highlighting. A highlighter marks what looked important while you were reading. That's a decision you make before you understand anything. It also leaves you with a yellow page and no answers.
Reading twice is slower than reading once and answering.

cards.question: Why turn headings into questions before you read?
choices: It gives you something to be looking for
cards.why: A question turns reading from scanning into searching. You notice the answer when it arrives, instead of noticing nothing.

title: The five-minute start
blurb: Procrastination is nearly always about starting, not about working. So make starting the only thing you commit to.
takeaway: You learned to commit to starting and let finishing follow.

cards.body: Putting something off is almost always about starting it, not about doing it.
So shrink the commitment to five minutes, and mean the part where you're allowed to stop.
Most of the time you don't stop. Starting was the hard part and it's behind you.
For an essay, the five minutes is opening the file and writing a bad first sentence. Bad is fine. It gets deleted.
Commit to starting, never to finishing. Finishing takes care of itself more often than you'd think.

cards.question: Why does the five minutes have to be a real permission to stop?
choices: Five minutes is enough for most work
If it's a trick, your brain stops falling for it
cards.why: The method works because starting is genuinely cheap. If stopping isn't allowed, starting costs the whole task again.

title: Your brain holds about four things
blurb: Working memory is the scratchpad you think with, and it is tiny. You'll see why a phone on the desk costs you a slot, and the one trick that makes four slots feel like more.
takeaway: You learned why one open tab is a study tool.

cards.body: Working memory is the scratchpad you think with. It holds about four things at once, and that's it.
Every open loop takes a slot. The song stuck in your head. The text you haven't answered. The phone face up on the desk.
When a fifth thing arrives, something falls off. Usually it's the thing you were trying to learn.
The trick is chunking: pack several items into one. 8675309 is seven things. 867-5309 is two.
Before a problem set, write the three formulas on a sticky note. Now they live on paper, and the slots are free for the actual problem.
Four slots. Everything you carry in your head is sitting in one of them.

cards.question: Why does a phone face up on the desk hurt studying?
choices: It keeps a slot busy even when it's silent
It only hurts if it buzzes
cards.why: An unfinished thing stays open in your head. It sits in a slot whether or not the phone makes a sound.

title: Why you can't stop scrolling
blurb: Feeds are built on the same trick as slot machines: a reward that only sometimes comes. You'll see why 'sometimes' hooks harder than 'always', and the one setting that breaks the loop.
takeaway: You learned that 'sometimes' is the hook.

cards.body: Pull down to refresh. Something might be there. Something might not. That uncertainty is the whole design.
Most pulls give you nothing. Then one gives you a like, a reply, a good post. You keep pulling for the next one.
A reward that comes every time gets boring fast. A reward that comes sometimes keeps you pulling longest. Slot machines run on exactly this.
The fix isn't willpower. Kill the surprise. With notifications off, nothing arrives unannounced, so there's no pull to answer.
Pigeons taught to peck for a seed every time stopped when the seed stopped. Pigeons rewarded at random kept pecking for hours.
The feed isn't fun. It's uncertain. Uncertainty is what you're hooked on.

cards.question: Which reward keeps a habit going the longest?
choices: One that comes on a schedule
cards.why: A random reward means every pull could be the one. There's never a moment where stopping feels safe.

title: The sunk cost trap
blurb: You paid for the ticket, so you sit through the bad movie. That's the trap. You'll see why money already spent shouldn't vote, and how to catch yourself doing it.
takeaway: You learned that only the future gets a vote.

cards.body: You paid $15 for the movie. Twenty minutes in, it's bad. Do you stay?
The $15 is gone either way. Stay or leave, you don't get it back. It shouldn't get a vote.
The next 90 minutes are still yours. That's the only thing the decision is about.
Sunk cost is when the past votes anyway. 'I've already put so much into this' is the sound it makes.
Three semesters into a major you hate. The credits are spent. The question is only whether the next three are worth it.
Money and time already spent are gone in every version of the future. Only what's ahead gets a vote.

cards.question: What's the right question when you're 20 minutes into a bad movie?
choices: Is the next 90 minutes worth it?
cards.why: The ticket is spent whatever you do. The only thing you still control is the time ahead.

title: Confirmation bias
blurb: Your brain lets in what agrees with you and waves off what doesn't. You'll see the filter at work, and the one question that gets around it.
takeaway: You learned to look for what would prove you wrong.

cards.body: Facts come at you all day. Some fit what you already think. Some don't.
The ones that fit sail through. They feel obviously true, so you remember them.
The ones that don't fit get a harder look, a shrug, or no look at all. You forget them by dinner.
So you end up more sure, not more right. The only way around it is to go looking for the fact that would prove you wrong.
You think your friend is mad at you. You'll notice the short text and miss the two normal ones. Ask instead: what would I see if they weren't?
You don't test beliefs by finding support. You test them by hunting for the thing that would break them.

cards.question: What's the best way to check whether a belief is true?
choices: Look for what would disprove it
Ask people who agree with you
cards.why: Support is easy to find for almost anything. A belief that survives a real attempt to break it has earned something.

title: Nobody is watching you that closely
blurb: The spotlight effect: you feel like everyone noticed, and they didn't. You'll see the study where people overestimated by half, and why it happens.
takeaway: You learned that everyone is in their own spotlight.

cards.body: You walk in wearing something embarrassing. It feels like a spotlight is on you and the whole room is looking.
But everyone else is standing in their own spotlight. They're busy with how they look.
In a famous study, students wore an embarrassing shirt into a room. They guessed half the room noticed. About a quarter actually did.
You overestimate by about double. The stumble, the wrong answer, the bad haircut. Half the people you think saw it didn't.
You are the main character of your day only. Everyone else is the main character of theirs.

cards.question: How many people noticed the embarrassing shirt, compared to the guess?
cards.why: Students guessed around half the room. About a quarter noticed. We overrate how much others see.

title: The habit loop
blurb: Every habit has three parts, and only one of them is the part you see. You'll find the cue and reward hiding around a habit, and learn to swap the middle instead of fighting all three.
takeaway: You learned to swap the routine, not fight the loop.

cards.body: A habit is a loop with three parts. It runs on its own, without you deciding anything, which is why it's so hard to fight head on.
Cue, routine, reward. Round and round. Every habit you have, good or bad, runs on this same loop. Once you can see the parts, you can work on it.
The cue is the trigger. You sit down on your bed after school, bag still on. Nothing has happened yet, but the loop has already started.
The routine is what you do. Phone out, feed open, thumb moving. It is the only part of the loop you actually notice, so it gets all the blame.
The reward is what you get. Twenty minutes of not thinking about anything. The loop runs to get this, and it will run again tomorrow.
You can't delete a cue or a reward. The bed is still there and you still need the break. But you can swap what happens in the middle.
Same bed. Same twenty minutes off. Different thing in your hand. A book, a sketchpad, a guitar. The loop still gets its reward, so it keeps running.
Bedtime scroll, after-class snack, the coffee you need before you can start anything. All loops, all built the same way. Look for the three parts.
Next time the habit fires, stop and ask three things. Where are you, what time is it, what just happened. That is the cue, and now you can see it coming.
Keep the cue. Keep the reward. Swap only the routine in between.

cards.question: Which part of the loop can you actually change?
choices: The cue, by avoiding the places and times that trigger it.
The routine, what you do between the trigger and the payoff.
The reward, by training yourself to stop wanting the payoff.
cards.why: Cues and rewards are wired in. The bed is still there and you still want the break. The routine in the middle is the part you get to pick.

title: Say 'I'm excited', not 'calm down'
blurb: Nerves and excitement feel the same in the body. You'll see why 'calm down' fails, and the two words that turned a racing heart into a better test score.
takeaway: You learned to relabel nerves instead of fighting them.

cards.body: Racing heart. Sweaty hands. Fast breathing. Your body does exactly this before a test, a speech, or a first date.
Call it anxiety and your brain reads it as a threat. Now you're nervous about being nervous.
Call it excitement and nothing in the body changes. Same heart rate, same hands. Only the label moved.
'Calm down' asks your body to do the impossible. 'I'm excited' asks it to do nothing. That's why it works.
In one study, people said either 'I'm calm' or 'I'm excited' before singing karaoke. The excited group scored about 80%. The calm group scored about 53%.
Your body can't tell nervous from excited. So tell it which one it is.

cards.question: Why does 'I'm excited' beat 'calm down'?
choices: It changes the label, not the body
cards.why: The racing heart stays. Calling it excitement stops you fighting it and points the energy somewhere useful.

title: Ask for an extension the right way
blurb: Teachers say yes to a good extension email far more often than students think. You'll build the four-line version: what, when, the specific ask, and proof you've started.
takeaway: You learned the four lines that get a yes.

cards.body: An extension email has four lines. Send it before the deadline, not after. That one detail changes the answer more than anything else.
Line one: what and when. 'The bio lab report is due Friday.' No story yet.
Line two: the ask, with a date. 'Could I turn it in Monday at 8am?' A specific date is easy to say yes to. 'A few more days' is not.
Line three: proof you've started. 'I've attached my draft with the first two sections done.' This is what separates you from the ones who haven't begun.
Line four: thanks, and stop. No paragraph about why. If they want the reason, they'll ask.
Ask early. Name a date. Show the draft. Skip the story.

cards.question: Which detail matters most in an extension request?
choices: Sending it before the due date
cards.why: Before the deadline it's a request. After, it's an excuse. Teachers treat the two very differently.

title: How to say no
blurb: A clean no is short, kind, and doesn't invite a negotiation. You'll see the three-part shape, and why a long excuse is the thing that gets you talked back into it.
takeaway: You learned that a short no is the kind one.

cards.body: Saying no feels rude, so most people bury it in a long excuse. The excuse is the problem, not the no.
Part one: something warm. 'Thanks for thinking of me.' It's true, and it costs nothing.
Part two: the no, plain. 'I can't this weekend.' No 'maybe', no 'I'll try'. A soft no gets treated as a yes.
Part three, if you want it: what you can do. 'But I'm free Tuesday.' Now it's an offer, not a rejection.
What you leave out: the reason. Every reason is a door. 'I have homework' gets 'do it after'. No reason, no door.
Warm, then no, then an offer. The excuse is what gets you talked back in.

cards.question: Why skip the reason when you say no?
choices: Every reason can be argued with
cards.why: A reason turns your no into a problem to solve. 'I have homework' invites 'do it later'. A plain no has nothing to push on.

title: Listen so people feel heard
blurb: When a friend is upset, the instinct is to fix it or cheer them up. Both make it worse. You'll learn the one move that works: say back what you heard, then ask.
takeaway: You learned to reflect before you fix.

cards.body: A friend says: 'I completely bombed that test.' What you say next decides whether they keep talking.
'You'll be fine' feels kind. It isn't. It tells them the feeling was wrong, and the conversation ends.
Try saying back what you heard: 'Sounds like it really got to you.' Nothing fixed. Nothing judged. They feel heard, and they keep going.
Then ask, don't advise. 'What part went wrong?' Advice comes later, if they want it. Most of the time they don't.
Reflect it back. Then ask. Fixing can wait, and usually isn't wanted.

cards.question: A friend says they bombed a test. What's the best first reply?
choices: 'Sounds like it really got to you'
cards.why: Saying back what you heard shows you listened. The other two close the conversation, one with comfort and one with a lecture.

title: Small talk without the panic
blurb: You don't need good stories. You need follow-up questions. You'll see the ladder that turns 'where are you from' into a real conversation, and the study on why askers get liked.
takeaway: You learned that follow-ups do the work.

cards.body: Small talk feels hard because you think you need something interesting to say. You don't. You need the next question.
Start anywhere. 'Where are you from?' Boring is fine. It's the bottom rung, not the whole ladder.
Then climb: ask about their answer. 'What do you like about it?' Now they're talking about something they care about.
Climb again. 'How did you get into that?' Three rungs in, it's a real conversation, and you've said almost nothing.
Researchers watched hundreds of first conversations. The people who asked more follow-up questions were consistently rated more likeable.
You don't need a good story. You need the next question about theirs.

cards.question: What made people more likeable in first conversations?
cards.why: Follow-up questions show you listened to the last answer. That's what people remember, not your stories.

title: A real apology has three parts
blurb: 'Sorry you feel that way' isn't an apology, and everyone can tell. You'll see the three parts a real one needs, and the two words that quietly cancel it.
takeaway: You learned what makes 'sorry' land.

cards.body: A real apology has three parts. Most people do one and wonder why it didn't work.
Part one: name what you did. 'I told people what you said in private.' Specific. No 'if I did anything'.
Part two: name what it cost them. 'That made it hard to trust me.' This is the part people skip, and the part that matters.
Part three: what changes. 'I'm not going to repeat things you tell me.' An apology without this is just a description.
The two words that cancel all of it: 'but' and 'if'. 'I'm sorry, but' means 'I'm not sorry'. 'Sorry if' means 'this is your problem'.
What I did. What it cost you. What changes. No but, no if.

cards.question: What does 'I'm sorry if you were hurt' actually say?
choices: That the hurt is their problem, not yours
cards.why: 'If' puts the feeling in doubt. It sounds like an apology, but it doesn't own anything.

title: Where your paycheck goes
blurb: Your first paycheck is smaller than the number you agreed to. You'll see exactly who takes what from $1,000, and why some of it comes back in April.
takeaway: You learned the difference between gross and take-home.

cards.body: You earn $1,000 in a month. That's your gross pay. It's not what lands in your account.
Social Security takes 6.2%. That's $62. It funds payments to retired people, and one day, to you.
Medicare takes 1.45%. That's $14.50. Together with Social Security, these are called FICA, and almost every worker pays them.
Income tax varies. It depends on the W-4 form you filled out and your state. For a student earning this little, often $0 to $100 of the $1,000.
What's left is your net pay, or take-home. Around $825 to $925 of the $1,000. If too much tax was taken, you get it back as a refund after you file.
Gross is what you earned. Net is what you get. The gap is FICA plus income tax.

cards.question: Which of these does every worker pay, no matter what?
cards.why: FICA comes off almost every paycheck at fixed rates. Income tax depends on your state and your form, and some people owe none.

title: Tax brackets aren't what you think
blurb: Moving into a higher bracket never costs you money. You'll see how brackets work like stacked buckets, and why a raise is always worth taking.
takeaway: You learned that only the top slice pays the top rate.

cards.body: Tax brackets are stacked buckets. Your taxable income (your pay minus the standard deduction) fills them from the bottom up. Each bucket has its own rate.
The first $11,925 you earn is taxed at 10%. That's the bottom bucket. Everyone's first dollars go here.
The next chunk, up to $48,475, is taxed at 12%. Only the money in this bucket pays 12%. The bottom bucket still pays 10%.
Above that, up to $103,350, the rate is 22%. Have $50,000 of taxable income and only about $1,500 of it is in this bucket. The rest sits in the cheaper ones below.
So a raise that pushes you into a higher bracket only taxes the new dollars higher. You never take home less by earning more.
Someone with $50,000 of taxable income doesn't pay 22% of $50,000. They pay 10% on the first bucket, 12% on the second, and 22% on the ~$1,500 that spills over. About $6,000 total, not $11,000.
Only the dollars above the line pay the higher rate. A raise never costs you money.

cards.question: You have $50,000 of taxable income and the 22% bracket starts at $48,475. How much is taxed at 22%?
cards.why: Only the money above the bracket line, about $1,525, pays 22%. Everything below it stays in the cheaper buckets.

title: A Roth IRA at 18
blurb: It's a jar where money grows for decades and comes out with no tax at all. You'll see why starting at 18 beats starting at 30 by a mile, and the one rule for opening one.
takeaway: You learned why the early jar wins.

cards.body: A Roth IRA is a jar for retirement money. Money you already paid tax on goes in. Then it grows for decades.
Inside the jar, growth is never taxed. The $2,000 you put in could become $20,000, and you owe nothing on the extra.
After 59½, and once the account is five years old, it all comes out tax-free. And the money you put in, not the growth, can come out any time without penalty.
The one rule: you need earned income. A summer job counts. Babysitting money counts if you report it. You can put in up to $7,000 a year, or everything you earned if that's less.
Put in $2,000 a year for seven years, 18 to 24, then stop forever. At 7% growth, that's about $250,000 at 65. Start at 30 and you'd need to save for decades to catch up.
The jar rewards years, not amounts. Seven years at 18 can beat thirty years later.

cards.question: What do you need before you can open a Roth IRA?
cards.why: Any earned income counts, including a summer job. Age and hours don't matter, only that the money came from work.

title: Why a dollar shrinks
blurb: Inflation is why the burrito that cost $8 now costs $10. You'll see what that does to cash sitting still, and why a savings account has to beat it to keep up.
takeaway: You learned why cash sitting still loses.

cards.body: In 2020 this burrito cost $8. Same burrito, same place.
In 2025 it costs about $10. Prices across everything rose roughly a quarter in those five years. That's inflation.
Your $8 didn't change. But now it buys about four-fifths of a burrito. The number stayed. The dollar shrank.
Cash under a mattress loses around 3% of its buying power a year, in a normal year. A savings account paying 4% stays a bit ahead. One paying 0.1% doesn't.
A dollar is a claim on stuff. If stuff gets pricier, the dollar gets smaller.

cards.question: You keep $500 in cash for five years. What happens to it?
choices: It buys less than it used to
cards.why: The bills say $500, but prices went up around it. The same cash buys fewer burritos than it did.

title: The trolley problem
blurb: A runaway trolley, five people, one lever. You'll see why almost everyone pulls it, why almost nobody pushes, and why that gap is the question behind self-driving cars and every triage rule.
takeaway: You learned that how a harm happens changes the answer, even when the count doesn't.

cards.body: A runaway trolley is coming down the track. The brakes are gone, and it is not slowing down. Nobody on board can stop it.
Ahead, the track splits in two. Which way the trolley goes depends on a lever beside the track. Right now it points down the main line.
On the main track: five people. They can’t get out of the way. If nobody does anything, the trolley hits all five.
On the side track: one person, just as stuck. And you’re standing at the lever. You have a few seconds to decide.
Pull it, and the trolley turns. One person dies instead of five. Ask a room full of people and most of them say the same thing: pull.
It feels like simple math. Five is more than one, so you save the five. Now change one detail and watch how fast that math stops working.
Same trolley. Same five people. But now you’re on a bridge over the track, next to a large stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, into its path.
Still one death instead of five. The math hasn’t changed at all. But almost nobody says they would push. Something else is going on.
At the lever, the one person dies because of where he was standing. A side effect. On the bridge, you use the man to stop the trolley. He’s the tool.
Five versus one is the easy part. What we actually argue about is whether a person was used.
This isn’t just a puzzle. A self-driving car has to be told what to do when a crash can’t be avoided. Someone writes that rule.
An emergency room decides who gets treated first when there isn’t time for everyone. Same argument, no lever. Real people.

cards.question: A surgeon could save five patients using the organs of one healthy visitor. Almost everyone says no. Which case is this most like?
choices: The lever. One life is traded for five, so the math is the same.
The bridge. The visitor is used as the means to save the five.
Neither. Medicine has its own rules, so the cases don’t compare.
cards.why: The numbers match the lever, but the visitor isn’t in the way of anything. He’s the tool that saves the five. That is exactly what the bridge case tests.

title: The ship of Theseus
blurb: Replace every plank on a ship, one at a time. Is it the same ship? You'll see the puzzle, the twist that makes it worse, and why your phone and your body are in it too.
takeaway: You learned that 'same' is a choice, not a fact.

cards.body: The Greeks kept the hero Theseus's ship in the harbour for centuries. Wood rots. So they replaced the planks as they went.
One plank at a time. After a while, a third of the ship is new wood. Still his ship? Sure, feels like it.
Eventually every plank has been swapped. Not one piece of the original is left. Same ship?
The twist: someone saved all the old planks and rebuilt them into a second ship. Now there are two. Which one is Theseus's?
Your phone with a new screen, a new battery, and a new back. Same phone? Most of the cells in your body get replaced over the years. Same you?
Same is not a fact about the thing. It's a rule we choose. Pick the rule, and the puzzle answers itself.

cards.question: Why is the rebuilt ship of old planks such a problem?
choices: Now two ships can each claim to be the original
cards.why: One ship has the history. The other has the material. Each has a real claim, and 'same' can't mean both.

title: Plato's cave
blurb: Prisoners chained to a wall, watching shadows, sure the shadows are the world. You'll see the oldest thought experiment about what's real, and why walking out hurts.
takeaway: You learned why leaving the cave hurts before it helps.

cards.body: Picture people chained in a cave since birth, facing the back wall. They can't turn around.
On the wall, shadows move. To the prisoners, the shadows are the world. They name them, predict them, argue about them.
Behind them, a fire, and people carrying objects past it. The shadows are just those objects. The prisoners have never seen the real things.
One prisoner gets loose and climbs out. The sunlight hurts. Everything looks wrong at first. When he comes back to explain, the others think he's gone mad.
A feed shows you a version of people: highlights, arguments, the worst clip of someone's day. It's easy to forget those are shadows of people, not the people.
The first taste of something real feels worse than the shadow. That's not a sign you were wrong to look.

cards.question: Why do the prisoners think the freed one has gone mad?
choices: The shadows are all they've ever known
cards.why: The shadows are their whole world. Anyone claiming there's something more real must be broken.

title: Notes you'll actually reread
blurb: Most notes get written once and never opened. You'll set up a page with three zones, so the notes quiz you later instead of just sitting there.
takeaway: You learned to make notes that test you.

cards.body: One page, three zones. Draw the lines before class starts. It takes ten seconds.
The big zone on the right is for class. Write what's said, fast and messy. Don't fix it live.
The thin column on the left is for after class. Turn each chunk of notes into a question. 'What does the mitochondria do?'
The strip at the bottom is one sentence that sums up the page. If you can't write it, you didn't get the class yet.
To study: cover the right side. Read the questions on the left. Answer out loud. Uncover and check. That's a quiz you built yourself.
Notes that can't quiz you are just a transcript. Add the question column.

cards.question: What goes in the left column?
cards.why: The left column turns the page into a test. Cover the right side and the questions are all you see.

title: Explain it to a twelve-year-old
blurb: If you can't explain it simply, you don't know it yet. You'll use a blank page and plain words to find exactly where your understanding runs out.
takeaway: You learned where your understanding runs out.

cards.body: Take a blank page. Write the topic at the top. Photosynthesis, say.
Now explain it in words a twelve-year-old would follow. No terms you'd have to define. 'The plant catches sunlight and uses it to turn air and water into sugar.'
Keep going until you hit a spot where the words go vague. 'And then it... does something with the light?' That's the gap. That's the exact thing you don't know yet.
Go back to the textbook for that one gap only. Fill it, then rewrite the sentence plainly. Repeat until there's no vague spot left.
Big words hide gaps. Plain words find them.

cards.question: What does it mean when your explanation goes vague?
choices: You found the exact thing you don't know
cards.why: Vague words are where understanding runs out. That spot tells you what to go back and learn.

title: Sleep is part of studying
blurb: Your brain files what you learned while you sleep. You'll see what happens in the early and late hours of the night, and why an all-nighter throws away the studying you did.
takeaway: You learned that the night does the filing.

cards.body: You study, then you sleep. Most people think the learning stopped when the book closed. It didn't.
Sleep runs in cycles, about ninety minutes each. Five or so in a full night.
The deep sleep comes early in the night. The best evidence says this is when the day's facts get moved from short-term storage into long-term.
The dream-heavy sleep comes late. This is when the brain connects new things to what you already knew.
Cut the night to four hours and you keep the filing but lose the connecting. Skip the night and you lose both. Studying at 3am is writing to a drive that won't save.
In studies, people who learned something and then slept remembered more the next day than people who learned it and stayed up, even with the same hours of study.
Sleep isn't the break from studying. It's the last step of it.

cards.question: What does an all-nighter before a test cost you?
choices: The filing your brain does overnight
cards.why: The facts you crammed never get moved to long-term storage. You read them, but they don't stick.

title: The first minute of a test
blurb: Most people start on question one and run out of time on question eight. You'll spend the first sixty seconds differently, and get the easy points before the hard ones eat the clock.
takeaway: You learned to spend the first minute looking, not writing.

cards.body: The test lands on your desk. Don't touch question one yet.
Spend sixty seconds reading every question. Just reading. Now you know what's coming and roughly how long you have per point.
Do the ones you're sure about first. Every easy point is worth the same as a hard one, and it's yours in two minutes instead of ten.
Mark the hard ones and skip them. Not stuck, just later. Coming back fresh, with the easy points banked, often makes a hard one look smaller.
Come back with the time you have left, and with the easy points already banked. A hard question you run out of time on costs nothing now.
Skim it all. Bank the easy points. Then spend what's left on the hard ones.

cards.question: Why skip a hard question instead of pushing through it?
choices: It keeps the easy points from running out of time
cards.why: A hard question can eat ten minutes and three easy questions with it. Bank the easy ones first, then come back.

title: Why $900 feels cheap
blurb: The first price you see quietly sets what every price after it feels like. It's called anchoring, and you'll watch it move the same jacket by $450.
takeaway: You learned that the first number drags every number after it.

cards.body: Two stores. Same jacket. The only difference is which price you happen to see first.
At Store A the first tag you see says $1,200. You haven't looked at the jacket yet. That number is already in your head.
Ask what you'd pay for the jacket and you land near $900. Not cheap. Just cheaper than the number already in your head.
Store B has the same jacket. The first tag here is $300. Now $450 feels like plenty to pay.
Same jacket, two answers, $450 apart. Nothing changed but the number you saw first.

Researchers spun a wheel, then asked people about the countries in the UN. Is the share of them in Africa higher or lower than the wheel's number? Then they had to name the real share. People who saw 65 guessed about 45%. People who saw 10 guessed about 25%.
The first number is not information. It's an anchor someone else dropped. Bring your own before you look.

cards.question: You're asking for pay at a summer job. Who ends up setting the range?
cards.why: The first number said out loud becomes the spot everyone argues around. So have your own number ready before you hear theirs.

title: Why they're a jerk and you're just busy
blurb: Their mistake means they're careless, but your mistake means it was a bad week. You'll see why the same act lands in two different boxes, and the one question that evens it out.
takeaway: You learned that you judge them by what they did, and yourself by what you meant.

cards.body: Something goes wrong. Your brain has two boxes to put the cause in. The person, or the situation. Every explanation lands in one of them.
A classmate snaps at you in the hall. You file it under person. They're rude. That's the box you reach for first.
The next day you snap at someone. You file it under situation. You barely slept and you were already late. Same act, other box.
Here's why the boxes split. You see your whole day. You saw one moment of theirs. The bad news they got at lunch never reached you.
The fix is one question. What's their situation? You're not excusing them. You're checking the box you skipped.

In a 1967 study, students read an essay praising Fidel Castro. They were told the writer had been handed that side and had no choice. They still leaned toward thinking the writer meant it. Psychologists call this the fundamental attribution error.
You judge them by what they did. You judge yourself by what you meant.

cards.question: A classmate bombs a test. You bomb the same test. How does the error usually go?
choices: They didn't study, and you had a bad week
You both had a bad week
cards.why: The bias leans one way. Their score becomes who they are. Yours becomes what was going on.

title: Losing $20 hurts twice as much
blurb: Losing $20 hurts more than finding $20 feels good. You'll see why an even bet feels unfair, and how that quietly bends your choices.
takeaway: You learned that losing hurts about twice as much as winning.

cards.body: This meter shows how money feels. The middle line is even. The same twenty dollars can push you up or down.
You find $20 on the sidewalk. That's a real lift. The meter goes up, but not all the way.
You lose $20 out of your pocket. Same amount, about twice the sting. It sinks the meter all the way down.
So an even $20 coin flip feels like a bad deal. Most people want about $40 on the win side before they take it. Twice the size, just to feel fair.

Credit card companies fought over the wording. They wanted stores to post a 'cash discount', never a 'card surcharge'. Skipping a discount feels like a smaller gain. A surcharge feels like money taken from you.
Losing $20 hurts about twice as much as finding $20 feels good. So an even bet never feels even.

cards.question: A friend offers a coin flip: heads you win $20, tails you lose $20. Why do most people say no?
choices: The $20 going out feels about twice as big
cards.why: The odds are even and the money is even. The feeling isn't. Twenty dollars leaving lands about twice as hard as twenty arriving. That makes a fair bet feel like a bad one.

title: Why rare things feel common
blurb: Your brain guesses how likely something is by how fast an example shows up. You'll see why the loud, rare stuff feels common, and the one question that fixes it.
takeaway: You learned that easy to remember is not the same as common.

cards.body: You're standing at the ocean. You ask how likely a shark attack is. Your brain doesn't count anything. It runs a search.
The first result is whatever was loudest. A video, a headline, a story someone told you. Shark attack comes back instantly.
The ordinary risks are in the list too. Drowning. A rip current. They almost never make the news, so they load slowly and sit near the bottom.
Here's what actually happens in the US. Sharks kill about one person a year. About 4,000 people drown.
So don't ask what comes to mind. Ask out of how many. A count beats a memory every time.
Think of English words with the letter R. Is R more often the first letter, or the third? Most people say first. It's third. First-letter words just arrive faster.
Easy to picture is not the same as likely. A quick example tells you what made the news, not what happens.

cards.question: You see two news stories about food poisoning at a chain. Why does the chain suddenly feel risky?
choices: You now have an example ready, so it feels common
You never liked the chain anyway
cards.why: Two stories hand you an instant example. Your brain reads 'came to mind fast' as 'happens a lot'. Two cases out of millions of meals barely move the real number.

title: How to disagree without a fight
blurb: Start with the part you think is wrong, and a disagreement turns into a fight. You'll learn two moves that keep it a conversation: say their point back, then name one thing.
takeaway: You learned to say it back before you push back.

cards.body: Your friend says practice should move to mornings because afternoons are too hot. You think mornings are worse. Most people lead with that, and now it's a fight.
Look at what they said again. Most of it you agree with. The heat is real. Find that part first.
Now find the one piece you actually disagree with. Not all of it. Just the piece: mornings.
Say the agreeing part back, in your own words. 'You're right, afternoons are brutal.' Now they know you listened instead of waiting to talk.
Then name the one piece. 'The part I'd change is mornings. Half of us can't get there by seven.' That's an edit, not a takedown.

Your friend says the group chat is dead because nobody plans anything. You think it's dead because the group got too big. Try: 'You're right, nobody's planning. I think the real problem is that there are forty of us in there now.' Same disagreement. No fight.
Say it back, then push back. And push on one thing, not five.

cards.question: Why say their point back before you disagree?
choices: It makes them forget their point
It buys you time to argue
cards.why: When people hear their own idea said back, they have less to defend. Your one disagreement then lands as an edit, not an attack.

title: Group projects that actually get done
blurb: Group work stalls when nobody knows exactly what to hand in. You'll see the three-column page that turns a vague pile into parts with a name and a day on each one.
takeaway: You learned that every part needs a what, a who, and a when.

cards.body: Make one page before anyone starts working. One row for each piece of work. Three empty columns: what, who, when.
Fill the 'what' column with things someone can hand over. Not 'research'. '10 slides on the causes.' An area can't be finished. A file can.
One name per row. Not two. When two names share a part, each one waits for the other. The part sits still.
Every row gets a day. Spread them out so the parts arrive one at a time. A part with no day gets started the night before it's needed.
All three columns live in one file. Everyone opens the same link. With three copies in three inboxes, the same work gets done twice.

In the 1880s a French engineer measured people pulling a rope. Alone, each pulled about 63 kg. In a group of eight, each pulled about 31 kg. Some of that is bad timing. Some is easing off when nobody can see your pull.
What, who, when, on one page everyone can see. Work nobody can point at is work nobody does.

cards.question: Which one belongs in the 'what' column?
cards.why: 'Sources' and 'look into' are areas. Nobody can tell when they are done. 'The timeline, drawn and labelled' is a thing someone can hand over.

title: How to ask for help
blurb: "I don't get it" gives the other person nothing to work with. You'll build the three-part ask instead: what you tried, where exactly you stopped, and what you want back.
takeaway: You learned the three parts of an ask people can answer.

cards.body: A good ask shows your path. Where you started, where you got stuck, and what you need to get moving. "I don't get it" shows none of that, so the other person has no idea where to start.
Part one: what you tried. "I watched the video and redid problem 3 twice." Now they know where to pick up, and they can see you put in the work.
Part two: the exact spot you stopped. Not "I don't get quadratics." Say "I get lost right where you take the square root." One spot can be answered in a minute. A whole topic can't.
Part three: what you're asking for. A hint, a check of your work, ten minutes at lunch. One small thing, not the whole unit. If you don't name it, they have to guess, and guessing is work.

Vague: "hey can you help me with the essay?" Nothing back for two hours. Specific: "I have the intro and two body paragraphs. My conclusion just repeats the intro. Can you read that last paragraph and tell me what's missing?" Answered in five minutes.
What I tried. Where I'm stuck. What I'm asking for. Leave one out and they have to guess.

cards.question: Which message is easiest for someone to answer?
choices: "Sorry to bother you, this is probably a dumb question"
"I'm stuck on question 4, step two. Can you check my setup?"
cards.why: It names one spot and one thing to do. They can help in a minute without asking you three questions first.

title: Why your texts sound cold
blurb: A text carries your words and nothing else, so the reader fills the tone in with their own mood. You'll see why 'fine.' lands colder than you meant, and how to type the tone in so it doesn't.
takeaway: You learned that tone has to be typed, not assumed.

cards.body: A text is words with nothing on them. The same 'fine.' can land warm or cold. The words alone don't say which.
As you type, you hear your own voice in your head. You already know you meant it kindly. So it feels obvious.
The reader hears nothing. They fill the tone in with the mood they're already in. Tired or stressed, and your text turns cold.
So there's a gap. You think your tone comes through about eight times in ten. Readers get it right about half the time.
So type the tone in. Say the good feeling out loud. Swap the cold period for something warmer. 'all good!' does the job your voice would have.
Students rated the exact same reply as less sincere when it ended in a period. 'Yeah' read like they meant it. 'Yeah.' read like they didn't. One dot did that.
Your voice doesn't travel with the message. If you want the tone read right, type it in.

cards.question: You text a friend 'ok.' and they think you're mad. Why?
choices: They filled the tone in themselves
cards.why: The words were clear. The tone wasn't in them, so the reader supplied one from their own mood.

title: Why the minimum payment is a trap
blurb: The minimum on a $1,000 card takes almost 6 years to clear and costs $766 in interest. You'll see where each payment goes, and the small change that cuts both numbers by about two thirds.
takeaway: You learned that most of your first payment is interest.

cards.body: You buy a $1,000 laptop on a credit card. The card charges 22% a year. You pay the minimum every month and nothing more.

This card's minimum is 1% of what you owe plus that month's interest, never under $25. Month one that is $28. Interest takes $18. That is rent for still owing the money. Only $10 comes off the $1,000.

Next month the minimum drops, because you owe less. After a year it hits the $25 floor and stays there. It takes 70 payments to clear the card. That is 5 years and 10 months of paying for a laptop you already own.
Add up every payment and you handed over $1,766. The extra $766 is interest. You paid 77% more than the price tag.
Now pay $50 a month instead of $28. Same card, same rate. You are done in 2 years 2 months and you keep about $500.

Your card statement has to print a box like this. It shows how many years the minimum will take. It also shows the bigger payment that would clear the card in 3 years. A 2009 law made card companies add it, after surveys found almost nobody guesses the real number.
The minimum is the slowest way the card lets you pay. Slow is exactly what makes it expensive.

cards.question: You owe $1,000 at 22%. Where does your $28 minimum payment go?
cards.why: Interest gets paid first. One month at 22% a year on $1,000 costs about $18. Only the $10 left over shrinks what you owe.

title: What an apartment really costs
blurb: Rent is only part of what an apartment costs you. You'll see the money due on move-in day, the bills that come every month, and what to have saved first.
takeaway: You learned that the listing price isn't the price.

cards.body: A listing shows one number. Say $1,200 a month. Two piles of money hide behind it: what you pay once, and what you pay every month.
Before you get a key, most landlords want first month's rent plus a deposit. That's $2,400 on day one. You get the deposit back when you move out clean.
Then the monthly extras. Power, water, and wifi run about $240. Renters insurance is $15 more, and it covers your stuff after a fire or a theft. That's $255.
An empty apartment is really empty. A bed, a table, a lamp, pots, a shower curtain. Even buying used, that's about $800.
Add it up. About $3,200 to walk in the door, and $1,455 every month after. The listing said $1,200.
Two roommates take a $1,600 place. Rent looks like $800 each. On day one they each hand over $2,000: first month, half the deposit, half the furniture. Then it's $935 a month each, not $800.
About three months' rent to get in the door. Then rent plus about 20% every month.

cards.question: The rent is $1,000. About how much should you have saved before move-in day?
cards.why: First month is $1,000. The deposit is usually another $1,000. Filling an empty apartment costs about a month's rent on top of that.

title: Chesterton's fence
blurb: A fence sits in a field for no reason you can see, so pulling it out looks obvious. You'll see why the missing reason is the problem, and the one question that earns you a say.
takeaway: You learned to find the reason before you remove the rule.

cards.body: A fence stands across an empty field. No sign on it. Nobody remembers who put it there. It looks like it does nothing.
So tear it out. It's in the way and nothing is using it. Chesterton said no. Not yet.
Fences don't grow on their own. Someone put this one here for a reason, and you can't see it from your side. Walk around it. There's an open well back there.
That's the whole test. Ask one question: why is this here? When you can answer it out loud, you've earned a say in whether it stays.
Your school makes everyone drop phones in a box before a test. It feels like they don't trust you. Then you hear a test got leaked last year and the grade had to retake it. That's the well.
You don't get to take the fence down until you can say why it went up.

cards.question: You find a rule that looks pointless. What does Chesterton's fence tell you to do first?
choices: Remove it and see what breaks
Find out why it was put there
cards.why: The idea isn't 'never change anything'. It's 'know the reason first'. Once you know it, you can keep the rule, fix it, or drop it on purpose.

title: Steelmanning
blurb: Beating the weakest version of someone's point proves nothing. You'll see how to build their side at its strongest first, and why that's the only version worth arguing with.
takeaway: You learned to argue with their best version.

cards.body: Any side of an argument has two versions. A flimsy one you could knock over in a second. And the one they actually hold.
A strawman is aiming at the flimsy one. You win, and nothing happens. You beat a version you made up, not the one they hold.
Steelmanning is the other move. Before you argue, build their side up. Say it back so well they'd tell you 'yes, that's exactly it.'
Now aim at that one. If it falls, you beat the real thing. If it holds, you learned something instead of winning.

Your friend says phones should be banned in class. The weak version: 'you just hate fun.' Easy to beat, worth nothing. The strong version: 'a phone in your bag still splits your attention, and it costs the struggling kids the most.' Now you have to actually think.
Aim at their best version, not their worst. Beating the worst one proves nothing.

cards.question: What makes a strawman useless even when you win?
choices: It's rude to the other person
You beat a version they never argued for
They can do the same thing back to you
cards.why: You knocked down something you built yourself. Their real point never got touched, so it's still standing.

title: You forget most of it by tomorrow
blurb: Most of what you learn today leaks out within a day. The drop is steepest right at the start, and you'll see how one short review turns the cliff into a slope.
takeaway: You learned that each review flattens the drop.

cards.body: You learn something today. The tall bar is all of it. The short ones are how much is still in your head on later days.
The empty boxes on top are what fell out. Almost all of the loss happens in the first day. After that it drains slowly.
Review it on day one and you are back at the top. One quick recall from memory, not a full reread.
Now the later days stay much higher. The cliff has turned into a slope.

In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself for a month. About a third was left after a day, about a quarter after a week. Class material you understand fades slower, but the shape is the same.
Forgetting is fastest right after you learn. The cheapest review is the soonest one.

cards.question: You read a chapter today. When is a ten-minute review worth the most?
cards.why: The steepest part of the drop is the first day. A review there costs the least time and saves the most.

title: Flashcards that actually work
blurb: Most flashcards fail because one card is carrying a whole paragraph. You'll see the three rules that fix that: one fact per card, the answer hidden, and the cards you miss coming back sooner.
takeaway: You learned that the cards you miss come back sooner.

cards.body: One card, one fact. Not a paragraph, not a list of six things. If you can't answer it in about five seconds, split it into two cards.
The answer stays hidden. Say it out loud, then flip. Reading the answer first feels like studying. Pulling it out of your head is what makes it stick.
Each box gets checked less often than the one before. Box one every day, box two every three days, box three once a week. That's a Leitner box.
Get a card right and it moves up one box. Get it right again and it moves up again. Each box up, you see it less often.
Miss it and it drops all the way back to box one. You see it again tomorrow. The cards you're worst at are the ones you see most.
Twenty Spanish words. After a week, fourteen have climbed to box three and you barely touch them. The six you keep missing sit in box one, and those are the ones you drill every day.
The cards you miss come back sooner. That's the whole trick.

cards.question: You miss a card sitting in box three. Where does it go?
choices: It drops back to box one
It moves down to box two
cards.why: A miss sends it all the way back to box one. It sits there until you get it right.

title: Your employer's match is free money
blurb: Your offer letter has a second number hiding in the benefits part. Here's what it's worth, why it beats anything you could buy, and the one catch to ask about.
takeaway: You learned that skipping the match means turning down part of your pay.

cards.body: You got the job. It says $52,000 a year. That's the number you'll tell people.
Now scroll down to the benefits part. There's a second number hiding in there. Almost nobody reads it.

First, what a 401(k) even is. It's a savings account for retirement that comes with the job. Money moves from your paycheck into it before you ever see it. It's your money. It gets invested, and you can't touch it until you're much older without paying a penalty.
A match means your job puts money in too, but only when you do. Jobs that offer one usually match your first 3% to 6% of pay. Say yours does 4%.
So your $2,080 becomes $4,160 on day one. Growing it yourself at 8% a year would take about nine years to do that.
Put in nothing and they put in nothing. That's not a bonus you missed. That's part of your pay you turned down.

One catch, called vesting. At some jobs their half isn't really yours until you've been there a year or two. Leave before that and you hand it back. Ask which one you're on during the offer call, before you sign.

Here's how you actually turn it on. In your first month there's a benefits sign-up, usually a website. You pick a percentage of your pay. Type in at least the number they match. It takes about five minutes and then it happens automatically forever.
Put in enough to get the whole match, even if you start at 1% and work up. Nothing else you can buy doubles your money on day one.

cards.question: Your investments had a great year and went up 12%. Why is the match still a better deal?
choices: The match doubles that money right away
You get the match whether you put in or not
cards.why: Up 12% in a year is great. The match is 100%, straight away. And the match only lands if you put money in first, so 0% in means 0% matched.

title: What to say when they ask your number
blurb: On the first call a recruiter asks what you're looking for. They already know what the job pays and you don't. Here's what that costs, and the one line that hands the question back.
takeaway: You learned to hand the number back instead of guessing one.

cards.body: It's your first call about the job. Usually a recruiter, before you've met anyone on the team. Near the end, they ask what you're looking for.
A recruiter is not your future boss. Their job is to fill the role, on budget. They're friendly because that's the work. It doesn't mean the conversation isn't a negotiation.
Here's what you can't see. Before that job was posted, someone approved a budget for it. A floor and a ceiling. The recruiter knows both. You know neither.
So you say $60,000. If their floor was $65,000, you didn't just aim low. You landed under the bottom of a range you never saw.

And the first number said is sticky. Everything after it gets measured against it. Say $60,000 and the rest of the call is about whether you get a little more than $60,000. Their $80,000 ceiling never comes up.
It also follows you. Raises are a percentage of where you started, so the gap widens every year. Ten years on, that one sentence cost about $57,000.

Ten minutes before the call fixes this. Check the job post first. A lot of states now make companies print the range. Then look up the title and city on levels.fyi. Then ask one person a year ahead of you what they got.
When they ask, ask back first. “What range is budgeted for this role?” It costs nothing, and plenty of recruiters will just tell you.
If they insist you go first, the research earns its keep. Say a range, and put the number you want at the bottom. Want $70,000? Say $70,000 to $80,000.
Ask before you answer. If you have to answer first, never say a number you wouldn't be glad to take.

cards.question: They won't give a range and want your number. You'd be happy with $70,000. What do you say?
choices: I'm flexible, make me an offer
cards.why: The lowest number you say is the one they'll work from. Put what you actually want at the bottom, so even the worst case is a yes. Saying $60,000 to $70,000 hands them $60,000.

title: Why asking at your review is too late
blurb: Raise money gets decided months before anyone tells you. Here's when that actually happens, what to bring, and the sentence that does the work.
takeaway: You learned to ask before the money is spoken for, with evidence instead of need.

cards.body: You've had a good year. So you wait for your review and ask there. That's the mistake almost everyone makes.
A review is the once-a-year meeting where your manager tells you how you did. It feels like the money meeting. It isn't. It's the meeting where you're told what was already decided.
Here's what you can't see. Months earlier your manager was handed a pot of money for the whole team and asked to split it. By your review, that split is done and signed off.
So the room where it's decided comes months before the room where you hear about it. Ask while there's still money to point at.
In practice that means the middle of the year. Not by email. Bring it up in a one to one, out loud, and say the word raise. Your manager needs to know before they walk into that planning meeting.
Bring evidence, not need. Rent going up isn't an argument. What you shipped is. What it saved is. What you now do that isn't in your job description is.
Keep a running list all year. One line every time something lands. You won't remember in October what you fixed in March. And a list written as it happened reads as fact, not as a pitch.
Then ask for a number, not a feeling. “I'd like to be at $78,000” beats “I was hoping for a bit more.” Say it, then stop talking. Let them answer.
If they say no, don't argue. Ask one question instead. “What would I need to be doing to get there?” Now you have a list. And a reason to come back with it.
Ask in the middle of the year, with a list and a number. Both halves matter.

cards.question: Your review is in December. When should you raise the money conversation?
choices: Around the middle of the year, before budgets are set
At the review, so it's on the record
Right after the review, for next year
cards.why: By December the pot was divided months ago. Mid-year is while your manager still has something to argue for, and still has time to argue for it.
